atoms.label: Reference frames, events, space–time and invariant quantities
atoms.summary: A reference frame is a coordinate-and-clock system for locating and timing events. An inertial frame is non-accelerating. An event happens at a particular place and time. Space–time combines three spatial coordinates and one time coordinate.
checks: Define the frame as well as the word inertial: “not accelerating” alone can leave half the definition missing.
Include time as well as position. A frame is not one point, and an event is not an object moving through space.

atoms.label: Why the Galilean prediction fails
atoms.summary: Compare the classical prediction with special relativity and explain the physical conflict. Galilean relativity itself says that Newton’s laws are the same in all inertial frames.
checks: Make the comparison explicit: explain how the Galilean result conflicts with invariant vacuum light speed or the speed limit for a material object.

atoms.label: Galilean coordinates and classical space–time assumptions
atoms.summary: Identify the two frames and use x′ = x − vt and t′ = t for the specified event.
checks: Name the frames and say which observer assigns each coordinate; an unlabelled description can miss what the transformation means.

atoms.label: Galilean velocity addition
atoms.summary: Calculate the classical prediction from signed velocities in stated frames, using u′ = u − v or its inverse.
checks: Choose the signs from the stated directions before substituting.
If the question explicitly asks for the Galilean prediction, calculate it even when it exceeds c. Explain the model’s failure afterwards.

atoms.label: The two postulates of special relativity
atoms.summary: State two distinct ideas: the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames; all inertial observers measure the same speed c for light in vacuum, independently of source motion.
checks: Keep the words “inertial” and “in vacuum”: vague versions have lost marks.
When using the light postulate to explain a result, state how the equal light speed supports that result. If asked to demonstrate it with an equation, show that calculation.

atoms.label: Choosing the right relationship
atoms.summary: Decide what is being measured, in which frame, and whether a supplied interval is proper. Then choose direct distance/speed, time dilation, length contraction, velocity addition, the interval or a Lorentz transformation.
checks: Use simple time dilation only when one of the two compared intervals is proper: the events occur at the same position in that interval’s frame.
Read a quantity directly when it is already given in the required frame. Avoid unnecessary length-contraction work, and do not apply another dilation to an already supplied clock reading.

atoms.label: Event separation or a measured length?
atoms.summary: Transform the same two events when their coordinate separation is requested. A measured object length instead uses endpoint positions taken simultaneously in the measuring frame.

atoms.label: Transforming one event’s coordinates
atoms.summary: Use the event’s x and t coordinates, the signed frame velocity and the common origin to calculate x′ and t′. If a coordinate is ct, keep its length units.
checks: Write the final transformed coordinates explicitly and retain their signs; a construction alone may not complete the answer.

atoms.label: Transforming the interval between two events
atoms.summary: Use Δx and Δt for the same ordered pair of events in one frame, then apply Δt′ = γ(Δt − vΔx/c²) and the corresponding space transformation.
checks: Use the actual spatial separation of the two events, with its sign, rather than a convenient but different distance.
Do not drop the position term by treating every interval as a simple time-dilation problem.

atoms.label: Calculating simultaneity and event order
atoms.summary: Calculate the signed time difference in the requested frame. Zero means simultaneous; the sign tells you which of your named events occurs first.
checks: Give the calculation or physical argument requested. Repeating an event order already supplied in the question earns no explanation credit.
Keep signed coordinates in your working and state the conclusion they support.

atoms.label: Calculating the Lorentz factor or speed
atoms.summary: Use γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²), or rearrange to v = c√(1 − 1/γ²). γ is at least 1; it equals 1 when the relative speed is zero.
checks: Check what a requested ratio represents. A length ratio may be 1/γ; it is not automatically γ or v/c.

atoms.label: Relativistic velocities in the same direction
atoms.summary: Identify the object and frame belonging to each velocity, then use relativistic velocity addition with consistent signs.
checks: Do not decide to add or subtract just from “same direction”. Which frame supplied each velocity matters.
Keep numerator and denominator signs consistent, and rearrange the equation for the velocity actually requested.

atoms.label: Relativistic velocities in opposite directions
atoms.summary: Choose a positive direction, assign signed velocities and calculate one object’s velocity in the other frame.
checks: Opposite directions require opposite signs in the starting frame; do not insert two positive speeds by habit.
Use the relativistic formula, not the classical sum, for the speed one fast-moving object measures for another.

atoms.label: Velocity comparisons, separation rates and invariant light speed
atoms.summary: Distinguish the gap’s rate of change measured by a third observer from the speed of one body measured in the other body’s rest frame.
checks: A separation rate above c does not mean that one object or signal travels above c. Do not confuse those two quantities.

atoms.label: Spotting a wrong velocity result
atoms.summary: Check the model, frame, signs and physical meaning of a proposed speed. Light in vacuum is measured at c; a material body’s speed in an inertial frame is below c.
checks: Do not accept a greater-than-c material-object speed, or a transformed vacuum light speed different from c.
If the question asks you to demonstrate the result using the addition formula, a remembered answer alone does not show the method.

atoms.label: A journey with a launched probe or second object
atoms.summary: Separate the stages of the journey. At each stage, label the object, the reference frame and the velocity before combining results.

atoms.label: Calculating the signed squared interval
atoms.summary: For two events, calculate (Δs)² = (cΔt)² − (Δx)². The two quantities cΔt and Δx use length units; their squares use squared length units.
checks: Keep a negative result negative. Do not silently take its absolute value or swap the two squares.

atoms.label: Explaining or demonstrating invariance
atoms.summary: Invariant means the same value in all inertial reference frames. To demonstrate it, calculate the interval for the same two events in both frames and compare.
checks: “It does not change” is too vague unless you say that you are comparing reference frames.
Do not discard an interval you have already calculated: its unchanged value can be used in the other frame.

atoms.label: Finding an unknown time from the interval
atoms.summary: Equate the interval in the two frames and solve for the unknown time. If the events occur at one position in the new frame, set Δx′ = 0.
checks: Use the zero spatial separation when the two events lie on the rest clock’s worldline.
Reuse the invariant value instead of treating the second frame as a fresh unrelated problem.

atoms.label: Finding an unknown distance from the interval
atoms.summary: Keep the same signed squared interval and rearrange for the unknown spatial separation in the requested frame.

atoms.label: Recognizing an interval shortcut
atoms.summary: Use invariance when it relates the supplied quantities directly to the missing quantity, especially when one frame has zero spatial separation.

atoms.label: Checking whether a signal can connect two events
atoms.summary: Compare the event separation with the distance light can travel in the available time. A required signal speed above c rules out the first event causing the second. When |Δx| > c|Δt|, different inertial frames can assign different event orders.

atoms.label: Proper time and proper length
atoms.summary: Proper length is measured in the object’s rest frame. For time dilation, proper time is measured in the inertial frame where the two events occur at the same position.
checks: “Same frame” is not enough: say rest relative to the object for length, and the same spatial position for the two time events.
Proper does not mean uniquely correct, and there is no universally stationary frame.

atoms.label: Choosing the proper quantity before calculating
atoms.summary: Name the two events or the two ends, identify the rest/same-place frame and label the supplied quantities before applying γ.
checks: Do not assume the “moving observer” must measure proper time. Identify the clock present at both events.
Check which way γ acts after identifying the proper quantity. Finding γ correctly is only the first step.

atoms.label: Choosing the right pair of endpoint events
atoms.summary: Ask whether you need an object length at one time or the coordinates of two specified events. Those can be different event pairs.
checks: For a length measurement, take both endpoint positions simultaneously in the frame doing the measuring.

atoms.label: Direct time dilation
atoms.summary: Identify the proper interval Δt₀ and relate it to the interval measured in an inertial frame where that clock moves, using Δt = γΔt₀.
checks: Do not calculate γ and then use it the wrong way round. Decide first whether you are finding the proper or dilated interval.
A clock ticks normally in its own frame. Say which other frame assigns it the slower rate.

atoms.label: Time dilation inside a longer problem
atoms.summary: Identify the events for the timing step, obtain the relevant interval in one frame, then apply time dilation only when its proper-time condition is met.
checks: Do not put arbitrary event-to-event intervals into Δt = γΔt₀ just because two frames appear in the problem.
atoms.classification_note: Journey, signal and muon tasks are counted in their more specific types. A zero here does not mean time dilation is absent from multi-step questions.

atoms.label: Journeys described in two frames
atoms.summary: Calculate each constant-velocity leg with a distance and time belonging to the same frame. Keep track of whether the question asks for one leg or the whole journey.
checks: Include every leg the question asks for; one outward leg is not a return journey.
Keep units consistent. Light years are distances; journey times are years or seconds.

atoms.label: Signals and arrival times
atoms.summary: Locate the emission and reception events. Allow for the receiver moving during the light’s flight, and distinguish elapsed travel time from the final clock reading.
checks: The receiver may move while the signal travels, so the initial separation divided by c may not be the catch-up time.
Add the emission-time offset when a clock reading is requested; a flight duration alone can be the wrong quantity.
Use the correct event coordinates and signs when transforming the signal’s interval.

atoms.label: Direct length contraction
atoms.summary: Identify the proper length and use L = L₀/γ for the component parallel to relative motion. Rearrange when the proper length is the unknown.
checks: Check which length or ratio is requested before multiplying, dividing or taking a reciprocal.
Keep both lengths in the same units. When the requested length is already readable in the right frame, read it directly instead of adding unnecessary calculation.

atoms.label: Fitting through a tunnel or past a marker
atoms.summary: Compare both lengths in one frame at one time. Identify which length is proper before calculating the moving length.
checks: Do not choose the proper length from the label “stationary” alone: identify the object or fixed marks whose separation is being measured.

atoms.label: Simultaneity and which event happens first
atoms.summary: Compare the coordinate times of the same two events in the requested frame and justify the order.
checks: Do not answer “seen first” when the question asks “happened first”.
Support a simultaneity claim with the events’ equal frame time, a line parallel to that frame’s space axis (x or x′), or the requested physical argument. A circular restatement is not an explanation.

atoms.label: Midpoint, lightning and beacon arguments
atoms.summary: Use the relevant frame, equal vacuum light speeds and the receiver’s motion to compare the signal paths.
checks: Make constant light speed part of the argument; naming the postulate elsewhere is not the same as using it here.
Track the correct signals and receiving event. Do not replace an emission comparison with light arriving at the wrong observer.

atoms.label: Happened first versus seen first
atoms.summary: Emission times are assigned to source events. Seeing times are when the light reaches a particular observer; propagation time connects the two.
checks: Read which order is requested. A nearer source being seen first does not by itself establish which source emitted first.
For reception order on a diagram, draw light rays to the observer’s worldline rather than guessing from the source positions.

atoms.label: Train-and-tunnel simultaneity explanations
atoms.summary: Identify the two endpoint events used in each frame’s fit statement. Lengths and simultaneity must be compared consistently within a frame.

atoms.label: Resolving an apparent contradiction
atoms.summary: Name the events and the frame behind each statement, then identify the different simultaneity assumptions. Use the constant-velocity situation actually specified.

atoms.label: Reading coordinates, order and simultaneity
atoms.summary: Read from the requested frame’s axes and scale; compare event times using that frame’s lines of simultaneity.
checks: Do not guess simultaneity or give a circular “same time” answer: use a line parallel to the requested frame’s space axis, x or x′.
Keep the simultaneous-event construction separate from the constant-interval calibration used to read the moving clock.

atoms.label: Reading light reception and clock times
atoms.summary: Find where a light worldline meets the observer’s worldline, then read the corresponding frame coordinate or elapsed interval.
checks: Do not confuse the emission point with reception. Trace the ray from the stated event to the receiving worldline.
Do not apply another time-dilation factor to a clock reading already given for that event in the required frame.

atoms.label: Plotting events, worldlines and light rays
atoms.summary: Place the stated events, start each worldline at the correct event and draw light towards later times. Label what the question requests.
checks: Do not force reception events into a pattern that sends a light ray backwards in time.
Start at the specified emission/departure event and include the required event label.

atoms.label: Drawing the moving frame’s axes
atoms.summary: Draw ct′ along the moving origin’s worldline and x′ along the line ct′ = 0, using the given relative velocity and common origin.
checks: Do not guess the x′ slope or rotate the axes in an arbitrary direction.
Start the axes at the specified common origin.

atoms.label: Using a diagram to transform coordinates
atoms.summary: Use lines parallel to the other primed axis to project the event, then read the calibrated primed coordinate and state the answer.
checks: Show the relevant construction or argument and give the transformed values explicitly, including their signs.

atoms.label: Speed from a worldline or angle
atoms.summary: Read the physical coordinate changes or, on equally scaled x and ct axes, use tan θ = v/c with θ measured from the ct axis.
checks: Use the axes and their units before applying an angle formula; read the coordinates accurately.
Check the worldline’s direction and physical speed. Negative x-velocity is allowed; a massive rocket faster than light is not.

atoms.label: Muon evidence: prediction and observation
atoms.summary: Use the given rest lifetime and journey data to make the non-relativistic prediction, then compare it with the muons actually detected.
checks: Use the data in this question instead of substituting remembered experimental numbers.
Explain how the lifetime and distance support the observed survival, rather than stopping at an isolated number.

atoms.label: Muon lifetime, travel distance and survival in the Earth frame
atoms.summary: Use the Earth-frame journey time and the dilated Earth-frame lifetime or half-life, then calculate or explain survival as requested.
checks: Label the frame and apply γ in the right direction; finding γ alone does not finish the explanation.
If survival is requested, use the lifetime or half-life after calculating the flight time.

atoms.label: Muon survival in the muon frame
atoms.summary: In the muon frame the muon is at rest and the atmosphere moves past. Use the proper lifetime with the contracted atmospheric distance and compare with the Earth-frame account.
checks: Do more than name length contraction: explain how the shorter atmospheric distance permits the observed survival.
Keep the frame attached to every time and distance so the two accounts remain consistent.
